articles.title: The Priest Who Sat Down
articles.dek: In 1954, a single operation in Boston did what no repeated treatment ever could. Hebrews says Jesus did the same with our sin, and then he took his seat.
articles.quote: The old altar kept an annual reminder of sin; the Lord's Table keeps a lasting reminder of the Savior who finished it.
articles.body:
On the morning of December 23, 1954, a 23-year-old named Richard Herrick lay in an operating room at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston, so poisoned by his failing kidneys that he had drifted in and out of confusion for weeks. In the room next door lay his identical twin brother, Ronald, healthy and about to give away one of his own kidneys. No surgeon had ever made a transplant like this work in a living patient. Dr. Joseph Murray and his team worked for hours, and when they finally released the clamps and Ronald's kidney filled with Richard's blood, it turned pink and began to work almost at once. Richard recovered, married Clare, one of the nurses who had cared for him, and became a father of two. Thirty-six years later, Murray received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for that morning's work.

To understand why that operation mattered so much, it helps to know what a kidney does. A pair of healthy kidneys filters roughly 180 liters of fluid from the blood every day, quietly pulling out waste and returning what the body needs, hour after hour, without a single conscious thought from their owner. When they fail, the poisons simply accumulate. Dialysis, which became a long-term treatment a few years after the Herrick operation, does the cleaning from outside the body. It is a genuine mercy, and it has kept millions alive, yet it can only borrow time. The patient sits for three or four hours, goes home, and feels the toxins slowly build again, and the next appointment is already on the calendar.

Many Filipino families know this rhythm from the inside. There is often a tito or a lola who leaves before dawn three times a week for the dialysis center, and the whole household arranges its life around those sessions. Every trip is a help, and every trip is also a reminder that the kidneys still do not work. A transplant brings a different kind of help entirely. It happens once, and afterward the cleansing goes on from within, every hour of every day, while the patient sleeps, eats, and goes to work.

That difference sits at the very heart of Hebrews 10. The letter was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who were growing tired and frightened. They had already endured public insults and the confiscation of their property (Hebrews 10:32–34), and many were tempted to slip back into the familiar rituals of the temple, which were safer, older, and visible. The writer, whose name we do not know, spends ten chapters showing them that going back would mean leaving the cure for the treatment.

To feel the force of the argument, picture the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of Israel's year, described in Leviticus 16. The high priest bathes and puts on plain white linen. A bull is slaughtered for his own sins, then a goat for the sins of the people. Carrying a pan of burning coals and a handful of incense, he passes behind the heavy curtain into the Most Holy Place, where only he may go, and only on this day. The smoke fills the dark room as he sprinkles blood on the gold lid of the ark, called the atonement cover. Outside, thousands wait in silence. Jewish tradition preserved in the Mishnah says the high priest kept his prayer inside short, so that the crowd would not panic that he had died in the presence of God. When he came out alive, the people rejoiced, and twelve months later they did it all again.

The writer of Hebrews looks at that annual drama and calls it a "shadow of the good things that are coming" (Hebrews 10:1). Then he says something surprising about what the ceremony actually accomplished: "But those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins" (Hebrews 10:3–4). Like a dialysis session, each Day of Atonement kept the people alive before God, and each one also told them plainly that the deeper problem remained.

"Day after day every priest stands and performs his religious duties; again and again he offers the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God." (Hebrews 10:11–12)

The furniture of the tabernacle is listed in careful detail in Exodus 25 through 30. There is an ark, a table for bread, a lampstand, an altar for incense, an altar for burnt offerings, and a bronze basin for washing. There is no chair anywhere in the list. The priests of Israel stood because their work was never done, and the next sacrifice was always waiting. When the writer says that Jesus "sat down," he is describing something no priest in Israel's history had ever done in the sanctuary. One way to read it is that the whole gospel can be seen in that posture: the Son of God took his seat because there was nothing left to offer.

There is a second treasure hidden in the Greek. The word translated "reminder" in verse 3 is anamnēsis, which means a calling to mind. It appears only a handful of times in the New Testament, and the other places are striking. At the Last Supper, Jesus took bread and said, "do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19), using that same word, and Paul repeats it in 1 Corinthians 11:24–25. This suggests that Jesus deliberately replaced one kind of remembering with another. The old altar kept an annual reminder of sin; the Lord's Table keeps a lasting reminder of the Savior who finished it. Meanwhile, God himself makes a promise about his own memory, quoting the prophet Jeremiah: "Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more" (Hebrews 10:17, from Jeremiah 31:34). God knows everything, so this is no lapse of memory on his part. It is a covenant decision never again to bring those sins forward as a charge against his people.

Verse 14 then holds two truths together with remarkable care: "For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy." The verb "has made perfect" is in the Greek perfect tense, describing a completed act whose results continue. The phrase "are being made holy" is ongoing, a process still underway. Richard Herrick's story helps here. His transplant was finished on a single December morning, and yet he still had to learn to walk the hospital halls, regain his strength, and build a life. His recovery was real and gradual, but it rested entirely on an operation that never needed repeating.

Many sincere Christians live as though they are still on dialysis. They confess the same old failure again and again, as though it had never truly been dealt with, and they come to worship hoping to feel clean enough to last until next Sunday. Confession still matters deeply, and Scripture invites it (1 John 1:9), but for the believer it is a child coming home to a Father who has already settled the matter, with no new sacrifice required. The writer says it as plainly as language allows: "And where these have been forgiven, sacrifice for sin is no longer necessary" (Hebrews 10:18).

So when an old sin rises in your memory today, perhaps something you have already brought to God many times, you can answer it with his own words and say aloud, "Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more." The next time you take the bread and the cup, let them be what Jesus meant them to be, a remembering of him rather than a rehearsal of your failures. You are allowed to rest, because your High Priest is already seated, and the work that saves you is being carried on inside you every hour, even while you sleep.

articles.title: The Word That Broke Twice
articles.dek: In one of the darkest chapters in the prophets, God uses the same word for smashing pagan altars and for what happened to his own heart. The people in exile who remembered that were the ones who found their way home.
articles.quote: Before a single altar on those hills was smashed, God's own heart had already been broken.
articles.illustration: Guo Gangtang's 24-year search for his son
articles.body:
In 1997, a two-year-old boy named Guo Xinzhen was playing outside his family's home in Liaocheng, in China's Shandong province, when human traffickers took him. His father, Guo Gangtang, did what every parent imagines doing and very few could keep up for long. He got on a motorcycle, tied a banner with his son's photograph to the back, and started riding. For twenty-four years he went from province to province, handing out flyers at bus stations and markets. He slept under bridges when the money ran out, wore out about ten motorcycles, and covered more than half a million kilometers of road. He was injured in crashes along the way and kept going anyway.

In July 2021, Chinese police used DNA testing to find his son, by then a grown man living in Henan province. The reunion was filmed, and millions of people watched a father in his fifties hold the boy he had last seen as a toddler while the two of them wept. Any Filipino who has stood at the arrival area in NAIA waiting for a parent coming home after years abroad knows what that embrace looks like. What made the footage so hard to watch was the father's face. Every one of those twenty-four years showed in it.

I thought of Guo Gangtang while reading one of the hardest passages in the Old Testament, because in the middle of it is a single verse where God lets us see his face.

Ezekiel was a priest who never got to serve in the temple. In 597 BC the Babylonians carried him off with thousands of Jerusalem's leading families, and he lived among the exiles beside the Kebar River in Babylonia. Back home Jerusalem was still standing, and many people believed the worst was over. Ezekiel's calling was to tell them it was still coming. In chapter 6, God tells him to set his face "against the mountains of Israel" (Ezek 6:2) and preach to the hills themselves. Those hilltops were where the people had built their "high places," open-air shrines to the fertility gods of Canaan, with altars and incense stands "under every spreading tree and every leafy oak" (Ezek 6:13). The sentence God gives is blunt. The altars will be demolished, the idols smashed, and the bones of the worshipers scattered around the shrines they trusted (Ezek 6:4–5).

Chapter 7 is darker still. "The end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land!" (Ezek 7:2). Ezekiel describes a city where the buyer has no reason to celebrate and the seller no reason to grieve, because neither of them will keep anything (Ezek 7:12). People will throw their silver into the streets, since "their silver and gold will not be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD's wrath" (Ezek 7:19). About ten years later, in 586 BC, Babylon burned Jerusalem, and every word came true.

Yet right in the middle of all this, the tone of chapter 6 shifts. "But I will spare some," God says, "for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the lands and nations" (Ezek 6:8). Then comes the verse that holds the passage together.

"Then in the nations where they have been carried captive, those who escape will remember me: how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts, which have turned away from me, and by their eyes, which have lusted after their idols. They will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their detestable practices." (Ezek 6:9)

The word the NIV translates "grieved" is the Hebrew nishbarti, from the verb shabar. It is an ordinary, physical word, used for breaking a clay jar, snapping a bone, or shattering a stone. Several translations keep that sense; the ESV reads, "how I have been broken over their whoring heart." What makes this striking is that Ezekiel has already used the same verb twice in this chapter. In verse 4, the incense altars "will be smashed," and in verse 6, the idols will be "smashed and ruined." Both are forms of shabar. The prophet seems to be setting two breakings side by side. The altars on the hills would be shattered by an invading army, and God says his own heart was shattered first, by the people he loved. Before a single altar on those hills was smashed, God's own heart had already been broken.

The phrase "adulterous hearts" tells us what kind of pain this is. The prophets often describe idolatry as unfaithfulness in a marriage (Ezekiel gives the whole of chapter 16 to that picture, and Hosea built his book around it). God speaks here as a husband who has been betrayed, and his anger in chapters 6 and 7 is real anger. The hurt underneath it is just as real.

What did the survivors remember? The verse says they will remember "me," meaning a Person. In a foreign country, with the temple gone and the land lost, they would finally think back and see the face of the One they had left. That memory leads to an honest, painful look at themselves ("they will loathe themselves"), and then on to something better: "And they will know that I am the LORD" (Ezek 6:10). One way to read this is that the turning point of their exile came when they understood what their wandering had cost God. They had probably known the rules all along. What finally brought them home was seeing his grief.

The rest of Scripture keeps returning to this same picture. Through Hosea, God cries out, "How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?... My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused" (Hos 11:8). Paul writes that "God's kindness is intended to lead you to repentance" (Rom 2:4). Jesus tells of a father who saw his son coming "while he was still a long way off" and "ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). That father had obviously been watching the road for a long time. Guo Gangtang watched the roads of China for twenty-four years, and the father in Jesus' story watched his road the same way.

This has a gentle, practical side for us. Most of us carry a small high place somewhere: a habit we defend, a resentment we feed, a source of security we lean on more than we lean on God. We tend to deal with these by feeling guilty for a while and promising to try harder. Ezekiel 6:9 suggests a better starting point, which is to remember the One we have drifted from and let ourselves see that our wandering matters to him. That honest sorrow is a doorway home, and the verse that follows says what lies on the other side: knowing him.

It shapes how we treat the people we love, too. Many Filipino families have a child, a sibling, or a spouse who has wandered, and our instinct is often to lecture or to go cold. The pattern in Ezekiel is closer to Guo's banner on the back of a motorcycle. God told the truth plainly, let his people see that he was hurting, and kept a way open for them to return.

Today, take a few quiet minutes to name one high place in your own life, and then tell God honestly that you know it has grieved him. Then do one small, concrete thing for someone you love who has drifted away. Send the message, make the call, or let them know you still miss them. The God who was broken over his people is the same God who spared a remnant and brought them home, and he is still watching the road for you.

articles.title: Seed Corn in the Smoke
articles.dek: In the darkest stanza of the Bible's longest psalm, a weary believer says he feels like a wineskin hung over the fire. He also tells us what the smoke could never reach.
articles.quote: God's word, kept in a smoke-dried heart, is seed being saved for the next planting.
articles.illustration: Lola's seed corn above the hearth
articles.body:
In many provincial homes, the real cooking still happens in the dirty kitchen out back, a lean-to of bamboo and yero where a wood fire burns under a blackened kaldero. Anyone who spent summers with a lola in the barrio remembers the smell of it, the smoke that settled into your hair and your clothes and the beams overhead. In some of those kitchens, if you looked up past the hanging ladles, you would see ears of corn tied together by their husks and hung from the rafters above the fire, so dark with soot that they looked abandoned.

A grandchild might ask why Lola keeps such ugly things up there, and the answer comes at planting season. She lifts a bunch down, peels back the brittle, sooty husk, and underneath, the kernels are clean, hard, and gold. Farmers across Asia, including families in our own mountain provinces, have long stored seed this way, because the steady smoke and dry heat keep away the weevils and the damp that would otherwise ruin it before the rains arrive. What looked finished on the outside was being kept, all along, for the next harvest.

Psalm 119 holds a picture very close to that one. It is the longest chapter in the Bible, a single poem built as an acrostic, which means it is arranged by the Hebrew alphabet. There are twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter, and every one of the eight lines in a stanza begins with that stanza's letter. The writer is never named, but he tells us enough about himself. He is a person under pressure who says that "rulers sit together and slander me" (Psalm 119:23), someone who loves God's word while living among people who mock it. Today's eight verses form the eleventh stanza, the one built on the letter kaph, and they are the lowest point in the whole psalm.

He opens with exhaustion: "My soul faints with longing for your salvation, but I have put my hope in your word" (Psalm 119:81). Then his eyes give out from watching the road for help that has not come: "My eyes fail, looking for your promise; I say, 'When will you comfort me?'" (Psalm 119:82). By verse 84 the question has become the cry every waiting person knows by heart: "How long must your servant wait?" His enemies are digging pits for him (Psalm 119:85). He is being persecuted "without cause" (Psalm 119:86). And then comes the line that tells us how close it was: "They almost wiped me from the earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts" (Psalm 119:87).

Right in the middle of all this, he reaches for an image from the kitchens of his own day.

"Though I am like a wineskin in the smoke, I do not forget your decrees." (Psalm 119:83, NIV)

In ancient Israel, wine and water were carried in containers sewn from goatskin. A fresh skin was soft and flexible, able to stretch as new wine worked inside it. Homes and tents of that time had no chimneys, so smoke from the cooking fire simply rose and drifted among the poles and rafters, and any skin hung up there slowly turned black, stiff, and cracked. Jesus drew on the same everyday knowledge when he said that no one pours new wine into old wineskins, because the old ones would burst (Matthew 9:17). When the psalmist says he is like a wineskin in the smoke, he means he feels dried out, shriveled, and darkened, a thing people would look at and assume was past using.

The Hebrew of this stanza makes his weariness even plainer. The word translated "faints" in verse 81 is kalah, which means to be used up, spent, brought to an end. The same root appears again in verse 82, where his eyes "fail," and once more in verse 87, where his enemies "almost wiped" him out. Three times in eight lines, the writer uses the language of being finished. He is honest about how depleted he feels, and Scripture lets that honesty stand without scolding him for it.

Yet every time he describes what the smoke has done to him, he adds what it has failed to touch. His hope is still in God's word (verse 81). He has kept from forgetting God's decrees (verse 83). He has held on to God's precepts (verse 87). The outside of his life is blackened, and the inside is still carrying what he put there in better days. Like Lola's seed corn, the very season that darkened him has also been keeping something safe within him.

There is one more detail in this stanza that is easy to miss. Psalm 119 has 176 verses, and verse 88, the last line of today's reading, is the exact halfway point of the entire poem. The darkest stanza sits at the very center. And the line that comes immediately after it, the first words of the next stanza, are these: "Your word, LORD, is eternal; it stands firm in the heavens" (Psalm 119:89). One way to read that arrangement is as a quiet message from the poet himself. He placed his lowest moment in the middle of the song, and he placed the firmest promise right beside it, so that anyone who reaches the bottom of verse 88 only has to turn the page to find solid ground.

Look, too, at how he ends his prayer. "In your unfailing love preserve my life, that I may obey the statutes of your mouth" (Psalm 119:88). "Unfailing love" translates chesed, God's loyal, covenant-keeping love, the kind that stays committed when everything else has given up. "Preserve my life" can also be rendered "revive me" or "give me life." A man who has just described himself as a dried-out skin asks God to make him supple again, and he asks for a reason. He wants to live so that he can keep walking with God. Even his request for rescue is shaped by the word he refused to let go.

Some of us know this stanza from the inside. You may be a caregiver who has not slept a full night in months, or a parent working abroad who sees your children only on a phone screen. You may be waiting on test results, on a visa, on a reply that never seems to come, or on a prodigal who has not yet turned for home. You may simply feel older and drier than you expected to feel at this point in your life. When you look in the mirror, you might see the smoke more clearly than anything else.

This psalm suggests that the smoke is only part of the story. Every verse you once memorized as a child, every promise you underlined in a hard year, every hymn your mother sang over the stove, is still in there. The fire that has worn you down has been unable to burn those things away, and in God's hands it may even be keeping them dry until the season when they are needed. God's word, kept in a smoke-dried heart, is seed being saved for the next planting.

You could carry that seed deliberately today. Choose one verse from this stanza, perhaps verse 81 or verse 88, and write it on a small card that you keep in your wallet or tape beside the sink where you wash the dishes each night. When you feel the old weariness rising, read it aloud, even if your voice is tired, and then pray the psalmist's own words back to God: "In your unfailing love preserve my life." He is a God who does not throw away blackened things. He hangs them where he can see them, and he knows exactly what is still golden inside.

Planting season does come. When it does, the Lord who kept your faith safe through the smoke will reach up, take you down from the rafters, and peel back the husk, and what he finds will be ready to grow.

articles.title: The Carpenter Who Stood Before a King
articles.dek: A village clockmaker spent forty years on one problem and finally found a hearing with King George III. Proverbs had already described a man like him, and the gospel goes further than Proverbs does.
articles.quote: Faithful work done in an obscure place is already being done before the King.
articles.body:
In the spring of 1772, an old man of seventy-nine waited on news from Kew, just outside London. His name was John Harrison. He had been born to a carpenter's family in Yorkshire, grew up in a small village in Lincolnshire, and never went to university. As a young man he built clocks almost entirely out of wood, choosing lignum vitae, a tropical hardwood so naturally oily that his gears needed no lubrication. That clever choice of material was the first sign of a mind that would not stop working on a problem until it was solved.

The problem he picked was one of the hardest of his age. Sailors could not reliably tell how far east or west they were, and ships were wrecked and lives lost because of it. In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of £20,000 to anyone who could find longitude at sea. The answer, Harrison believed, was a clock that kept perfect time on a rolling, salty, freezing and sweltering ship. He spent the next four decades building one. His fourth timekeeper, about the size of a large pocket watch, sailed to Jamaica in 1761 and lost only about five seconds over a voyage of more than eighty days.

The Board of Longitude kept moving the goalposts and held back most of the prize anyway. At last Harrison's son William wrote to King George III, who had a deep interest in science. The king tested Harrison's fifth watch at his own observatory at Kew for ten weeks, and it erred by only a few seconds. He is said to have told William, "By God, Harrison, I will see you righted!" In 1773 Parliament awarded the old carpenter £8,750. A craftsman from a village workshop had ended up in the presence of a king, carried there by the quality of what his hands had made.

Nearly three thousand years earlier, a teacher in Israel wrote a single line that describes Harrison's story.

"Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank." (Proverbs 22:29, NIV)

This verse sits in a distinct part of Proverbs. Beginning at 22:17, the book introduces what it calls "the sayings of the wise," a collection of about thirty short teachings (22:20). Scholars have long observed that this section echoes an older Egyptian school text, the Instruction of Amenemope, which closes by saying that a scribe skilled in his office will be found worthy to serve at court. Israel's teachers were happy to borrow good wisdom wherever they found it, but they set it inside a new frame. These sayings are given, verse 19 says, "so that your trust may be in the LORD." The skilled worker in verse 29 belongs to a world where the true King is God himself.

The Hebrew word translated "skilled" is mahir. Its root carries the idea of quickness, the ease of someone so practiced that the work flows. The same word describes Ezra as "a teacher well versed in the Law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6), and the psalmist says his tongue is "the pen of a skillful writer" (Psalm 45:1). Mahir is the fluency that comes from years of patient repetition, the sureness of a seamstress whose stitches run straight without a guide line or a mechanic who can hear what is wrong with an engine. Talent may get a person started, but this kind of skill is grown slowly in ordinary hours.

The phrase "officials of low rank" is literally something like "obscure ones," people who live in the shadows. The proverb's promise is that excellent work tends to rise into the light. Scripture shows this again and again. Joseph, a forgotten prisoner, interpreted dreams with such wisdom that Pharaoh set him over Egypt (Genesis 41:39 to 41). Daniel and his friends were found "ten times better" than the king's advisers (Daniel 1:20). Bezalel was filled with God's Spirit "with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills" to build the tabernacle where God would dwell (Exodus 31:3).

Proverbs is honest, though, that this is a general pattern of God's world and not a guarantee for every Tuesday. Harrison waited forty years, and some faithful craftsmen never get their audience with a king at all. Many Filipinos know this from experience: the nurse abroad whose excellence is overlooked, the teacher in a far-flung school whose name will never trend, the father who repairs aircon units with real care in a city that takes him for granted. If the verse ended with earthly palaces, it would leave many of us still waiting at the door.

The gospel carries the proverb further than its first readers could have imagined. When the true King came into the world, he did not first appear in a palace. He grew up in Nazareth, and his neighbors knew him as "the carpenter" (Mark 6:3). The Greek word there, tekton, means a builder or craftsman who works with wood and stone. For most of his earthly life, the Son of God was a skilled worker in an obscure town, measuring beams and fitting joints for people who had no idea who was serving them. The King of kings chose to stand in the workshop before he stood before Pilate.

That changes how a Christian can see the ordinary job. Paul writes to believers, many of them slaves with no hope of promotion, "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters" (Colossians 3:23). One way to read Proverbs 22:29 in light of Christ is this: the skilled worker who belongs to Jesus already serves before a King, because the King is present in every room where his people work. Faithful work done in an obscure place is already being done before the King. The audience Harrison waited forty years to receive is given to every believer on the first morning of their new life, freely, because of what Jesus did on the cross.

This also frees us from a heavy burden. Many of us quietly treat our work as the way to earn our worth, and so we either burn out chasing recognition or grow bitter when it never comes. The gospel settles the question of worth before we pick up a single tool. We are accepted in Christ, so we can afford to become excellent slowly, to care about small details no one will check, and to keep going when the board keeps moving the goalposts. Skill grown from that kind of security tends to be steadier and kinder, because it has nothing to prove.

The practical path toward mahir is usually humble. Choose one part of your work this week that you have been doing carelessly, perhaps the way you answer messages, the neatness of a report, or the patience you give a difficult customer, and do it with full attention as an offering to Christ. Ask God for the wisdom he gave Bezalel, and then practice. Over months and years, those small acts of faithfulness become fluency, and fluency becomes the kind of quiet excellence that often opens doors you never expected.

John Harrison's watch is still kept at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, and people travel across the world to look at it. His long years in the workshop were never wasted, even when no one important seemed to be watching. Yours are not wasted either. Pick up today's work, whatever it is, and do it well, knowing that you already work in the presence of the King who once worked with his hands.
